cards.title: The Merge button is offered while the gate runs — and while the Verifier says FAIL
cards.description:
> ## THIRD SIGHTING, 2026-08-23 — a new state, and the worst one yet: **the button is offered on DRAFT PRs**
>
> **Operator, looking at the board:** *"should I merge it?"* on #178. The correct answer was no, and the console was the reason they had to ask.
>
> Two of the seven open PRs were rendered with an **active blue Merge button**, and **both were drafts**:
>
> | PR | Console said | Truth |
> | -- | -- | -- |
> | bureau-pipeline #178 | *"At merge gate"* + **active Merge** | `isDraft: true`. Held as a draft **on purpose** — its own body says merging it before three consumer repos repoint *breaks those consumers* |
> | portico #343 | *"At merge gate"* + **active Merge** | `isDraft: true`. Held for the canonical channel guard |
>
> Every other row that day showed a greyed button. **The two PRs least safe to merge were the only two offering the action.**
>
> ### Why this variant is worse than the first two
>
> The earlier sightings offered a button on a PR that was *going to merge anyway* (redundant touch), then on one the Verifier had *proved broken* (merging a defect). This one offers it on a PR **deliberately held back**, where the draft flag is the entire mechanism preventing an out-of-order merge that has a written, known blast radius.
>
> And the failure is not ambiguous or verdict-shaped like the `call / verify` trap below. `isDraft` **is a plain boolean on the PR object the console already fetches.** There is no missing signal to plumb, no comment to parse, no gate to teach. The console reads `mergeStateStatus: CLEAN` plus "at merge gate" and never checks a field it already has.
>
> ### What clicking it would actually do
>
> GitHub refuses `PUT /merges` on a draft, so the optimistic case is a raw API error surfaced to the operator — the exact failure [DRE-2069](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2069>) already fixed once for stale rows. The pessimistic case is a merge path that marks the PR ready first and then merges, which would **silently defeat a deliberate hold**. Which of the two happens has not been tested, and nobody should learn the answer by clicking.
>
> ### Add to the state table above
>
> | Pipeline state | What the human should see |
> | -- | -- |
> | **PR is a draft** | **No merge action, in any circumstance.** "Held as a draft" — and, if the body states a reason, that reason. Not even the override arm: a draft is an author's explicit hold, and the override exists for when the *pipeline* is dead, not for overruling a deliberate one |
>
> ### Acceptance, extended
>
> - [ ] A draft PR offers no merge action, and the row says it is held as a draft
> - [ ] The draft check is derived from `isDraft` on the PR, not inferred from checks or `mergeStateStatus`
>
> **Fourth occurrence of** `inferred-from-adjacent-signal` (after [DRE-2530](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2530/the-actions-budget-alarm-cannot-see-the-block-it-exists-for-it-watched), [DRE-2537](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2537/the-console-says-fix-agent-working-when-no-fix-agent-is-working), and the second sighting). The pattern named at the bottom of this card is not slowing down, and this instance needed no new signal at all — only for the console to read a field it already had.

> ## SECOND SIGHTING, 2026-08-19 — and it is worse than the first
>
> **Operator:** *"#2070 is still asking to be merged… the merge button should not be active if there is an issue with the QA and the Verifier."*
>
> The original case below was *a button offered while the gate was already merging* — an invitation to a redundant touch. **Tonight's is a button offered on a PR the Verifier has proved broken.** Clicking it would have merged a defect the Verifier measured in a live browser.
>
> ### What the console showed, and what was true
>
> |  |  |
> | -- | -- |
> | Console | *"At merge gate"* + an **active blue Merge button** |
> | `QA critic review` | **pass** — the critic approved |
> | `QA Verifier` verdict | **FAIL** — measured in Playwright against a running console |
> | `mergeStateStatus` | **CLEAN** |
>
> ### THE MECHANISM — the console cannot see the failure
>
> ```
> call / review    pass   5m10s
> call / verify    pass   14m6s   ← the run whose VERDICT was FAIL
> ```
>
> `call / verify` **publishes** `pass` **for a run that returned FAIL.** The check reports that the Verifier *ran*, not that it *passed* — **the identical trap already recorded for** `call / review`, one gate over.
>
> So every check is green, `mergeStateStatus` is CLEAN, and **the FAIL exists only in a PR comment.** The console is not being careless: *it has no signal to gate on.* Any consumer reading checks — the console, a human scanning the PR page, a future automation — sees a mergeable PR.
>
> **This is why the fix cannot be console-side alone.** Greying the button requires the verdict to be *visible*, and today it is not:
>
> 1. **The verdict must reach a check** — a FAIL verdict publishes a failing status, so `mergeStateStatus` stops saying CLEAN and every reader benefits, not just the console.
> 2. **Then** the button gates on it.
>
> Doing (2) without (1) builds a console that reads a comment to decide, which is exactly the fragile comment-parsing the estate has been moving away from.
>
> ### Why this is Urgent rather than High
>
> The first sighting risked a redundant touch on a PR that was going to merge anyway. **This one risks merging code a gate has proved defective**, and the operator was looking at a blue button while it was true. Raised to Urgent.
>
> ### The rule, stated for whoever builds it
>
> **A green check must mean the gate PASSED, never merely that it RAN.** Where a gate's verdict lives in a comment, the check is decoration — and a decoration that reads as a guarantee is worse than no check at all.

**Observed live, 2026-08-18 21:18 PT.** PR #2064 had a critic APPROVE and the merge gate was **actively running**. The console showed it correctly — *"At merge gate"* — **and offered a Merge button next to it.**

The CEO did not click it, and asked for this card instead.

## Why an available button is the defect

The whole design is *nobody human clicks merge in the normal flow*, and the headline metric is **cards reaching Done with zero human touches**. A button presented at the exact moment the pipeline is doing the job is an invitation to spend that metric for no reason.

It is worse than a cosmetic problem, because clicking it during a live gate can be actively harmful:

* **It can merge a stale branch.** Seconds after this was observed, the gate updated #2064's head from `7e1dcd56` to `1b5f18cc` — the branch was behind `main` and [DRE-1924](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-1924/prevent-red-main-require-a-pr-branch-up-to-date-with-main-green-before)'s rule is *a stale branch is updated, never merged blind*. A human clicking Merge in that window merges code whose CI ran against a different base.
* **It bypasses the carried-verdict logic** that decides whether an approval still applies to the current head.
* **It costs the walk-away number.** Wave 0's demo clause — *"fails if any card needed a human touch to close"* — **failed**, partly on hand-merges. Every avoidable click makes that number worse for no gain.

## The button must NOT be removed

It was the only path that worked on 2026-08-18 21:38 PT: the Actions billing block killed the merge gate three seconds after the critic approved #2062, the gate never re-fired, and the CEO merging by hand was the correct action. Removing the affordance would have left that PR stranded overnight.

**So the fix is not removal. It is that the button's presence and wording must reflect whether the pipeline is handling it.** This is *escalate by exception* applied to a control: the human path stays available and stops being the default-looking one.

## What it should distinguish

| Pipeline state | What the human should see |
| -- | -- |
| Gate running, or a fresh APPROVE with a gate run pending | **No merge action.** "The gate is merging this" — nothing to do |
| Gate refused for a stated reason (stale, verdict mismatch, CI red) | Show the reason. Merge stays hidden — the reason is the next action |
| **Gate cannot run at all** (billing block, workflow disabled, App quota) | **Merge, prominently, labelled as the override it is** — this is the 21:38 case |
| Merged | The receipt, with `mergedAt` |

The distinction is between *the pipeline has this* and *the pipeline is dead and you are the fallback*. Today they render identically.

## Scope

1. **Red first** — a test that a PR with a live merge-gate run offers no merge action.
2. Derive the affordance from **gate run state**, not from "is this PR mergeable" — the same rule-1 error as [DRE-2537](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2537>): an adjacent signal (GitHub says mergeable) rendered as a different fact (you should merge it).
3. When it IS offered, **label it as an override** and say why the pipeline cannot do it.
4. **Record every hand-merge** so the walk-away metric can count them and each one has a stated reason. A hand-merge is not forbidden; an *unexplained* one is.

## Acceptance

- [ ] No merge action while a gate run is live for that head
- [ ] The override appears when the gate genuinely cannot run, and says why
- [ ] Each of the four states above renders distinguishably
- [ ] Hand-merges are counted, with reasons, and feed the walk-away metric
- [ ] Verified against a real PR in each state

## Related

Third sighting this week of `inferred-from-adjacent-signal` — after [DRE-2530](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2530>) (budget monitor publishing all-clear during a live outage) and [DRE-2537](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2537>) ("Fix agent working" with no fix agent running). **Three occurrences is past the threshold [DRE-2536](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2536>) sets for a pattern to stop being a note and become a gate.**

cards.title: The console says "Fix agent working" when no fix agent is working
cards.description:
**Observed live, 2026-08-19 \~03:40 PT.** The Open PRs panel showed **"Fix agent working"** against three PRs — #2054, #2063, #2064. **No fix agent was running on any of them.**

| PR | Console said | Actually |
| -- | -- | -- |
| #2054 | Fix agent working | REQUEST_CHANGES since 17:03 the previous day; fix loop **holding** on an unanswered blocker for **12 hours** |
| #2063 | Fix agent working | REQUEST_CHANGES; a human was fixing it by hand |
| #2064 | Fix agent working | REQUEST_CHANGES; nothing running |
| #163 | CI running | **already merged** |

## Why it is the worst possible wrong answer

"Fix agent working" means *stand back, the machine has this*. Every one of those PRs actually needed a person — and #2054 needed **one comment** to release a hold on a question whose answer had stopped being true an hour earlier.

**A stall that reports itself as progress is worse than a stall that reports nothing.** Silence at least invites a look. This actively told the CEO to wait, for twelve hours, on a PR nothing was coming for.

This is `standards/console-honesty.md` rule 1 in the negative: *"Derive from truth, never infer from adjacent signals."* A REQUEST_CHANGES verdict on an `agent/*` branch is an adjacent signal meaning *a fix agent is eligible* — the panel renders it as *a fix agent is running*. Those are different facts with different next actions, exactly the distinction that rule exists to protect.

## The states that are being collapsed

At least five, and they want different things from the reader:

1. **A fix run is genuinely in flight** — wait.
2. **A fix run is queued** — wait.
3. **The loop is HOLDING on an unanswered blocker** — **the CEO must answer.** This is #2054, and it is invisible today.
4. **The convergence halt has fired** ([DRE-2024](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2024/reconcile-re-dispatches-a-doomed-agent-fix-every-sweep-for-a-needs), two no-progress runs on one head) — the loop has given up; a human must take it.
5. **A verdict stands with no run at all** — nothing is coming.

Only 1 and 2 are "working". **3 and 4 are the CEO's queue and currently render as someone else's problem.**

## What it should read from

The truth is available and cheap:

* `gh run list --workflow agent-fix.yml` — is a run live, and on which head?
* The `🛑 Fix attempt N blocked` comment — the loop holding, and what it is waiting for.
* The convergence-halt marker — the loop has stopped for good.
* The verdict's anchored SHA vs the PR head — whether the standing verdict even applies to the current code.

## Scope

1. **Red first** — a test that a PR with a standing REQUEST_CHANGES and no live fix run does NOT render as "Fix agent working".
2. Derive the row from run state and the blocker comments, not from the verdict alone.
3. **A holding loop renders as a CEO action**, naming what it is waiting for. That state is why #2054 sat for 12 hours.
4. **Unknown renders as unknown** (rule 2) — "can't tell" is a legitimate and useful answer; a confident wrong one is not.
5. Stale-data test per rule 3.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Each of the five states above renders distinguishably
- [ ] A holding fix loop appears in the CEO's queue, naming the question
- [ ] No row claims work is in progress without a live run to point at
- [ ] Verified against a real PR in each state, not only fixtures

## Related

* This is the Layer 0 thesis in miniature: **the machinery detects almost everything and reports almost nothing** — and here it reports something worse than nothing.
* [DRE-2531](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2531>)'s blocking dialog covers *pipeline stopped, only the CEO can restart it*. A holding fix loop is quieter than that and needs a surface of its own — the Alerts panel, not a modal.
* Pattern candidate for [DRE-2536](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2536>)'s ledger: `inferred-from-adjacent-signal`. Its second sighting this week; [DRE-2530](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2530/the-actions-budget-alarm-cannot-see-the-block-it-exists-for-it-watched)'s budget monitor publishing all-clear during a live outage was the first.

cards.title: The learning ledger — make a lesson survive as a test, and measure whether we stop repeating it
cards.description:
**Operator, 2026-08-19:** *"The next day we relearn the lessons again and again. The agents never capture that knowledge, so the next cycle they don't do the same problem… We need to codify its learning and what we've changed to make it better. Another KPI is those errors going down that we see again and again."*

## The problem, stated precisely

**An agent has no memory. Every "lesson" is retrieval, re-delivered in full, every run, forever.** Nothing an agent experiences changes it. So a lesson only persists if something outside the agent carries it.

Today the critic finds a defect, the fix agent repairs that PR, and **the finding dies in a PR comment.** The next card gets a fresh agent that can make the same mistake, and nothing anywhere knows it is the second time.

## The trap: "write it in the standards" makes it worse

The obvious remedy is more instruction. **Instructions have a budget and we are already overdrawn.** The diagnosis measured it: an engineer on portico reads **\~1,280 lines** of standing instruction before it reaches the card. `adr-cost-emergency-prompt-reduction.md` once cut a `CLAUDE.md` from 201 lines to 35 *as a cost emergency*; portico's is now 457.

Every lesson written as prose competes with the card's own argument. Finding 15 this week was an agent building the architecture its card **explicitly rejected** — on one of the best-written cards in the corpus. More prose would not have helped it.

## The hierarchy — a rule is the weakest possible memory

| Form | Context cost | Can be ignored | Evidence from 2026-08-18/19 |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| **Rule** in standards | every run, forever | yes | `console-honesty.md` rule 3 — the pipeline's fix agent complied and cited it; the interactive session never received it and shipped a component with no stale-data test |
| **Test** | none | no | The banned model ([DRE-2526](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2526/take-the-banned-model-off-the-consoles-ladder-and-unpin-the-test)) **cannot recur** |
| **Gate** | none | structurally impossible | Branch-name matching; the AST guard on the WIP cap |

**So: a lesson becomes a TEST or a GATE wherever it can, and a rule only where it genuinely cannot.**

* *"Never route around a harness block"* — cannot be a test. Rule.
* *"Every state element ships with a stale-data test"* — **can** be a gate: fail CI when a component reads a query and has no stale-path test. Zero context cost, unskippable, and it would have caught this week's defect against an author who had never read the standard.

## What to build

### 1. The ledger — one row per finding

The critic already tags every verdict `cause:defect` / `cause:unmet-criteria` / `cause:scope`. **Nothing counts them.** Record, per finding:

| Field | Why |
| -- | -- |
| `at`, `repo`, `pr`, `card` | when and where |
| `cause` | the critic's existing coarse tag |
| `pattern` | **a short slug naming the RECURRING SHAPE** — the load-bearing field |
| `surface` | file/module, so hot spots surface |
| `fix_attempts`, `fix_outcome` | did the loop repair it, or a human |
| `remedy_type` | `test` | `gate` | `rule` | `none-yet` |
| `remedy_ref` | the test, guard or standards line that now defends it |
| `recurred_after_remedy` | **the only field that proves the loop closed** |

### 2. The taxonomy — and the trap inside it

`cause:` is too coarse to learn from. The real shapes this week were finer: *a signal nobody reads*, *a comment asserting an untrue agreement*, *a missing stale-data test*, *a card that closes with work outstanding*, *a mechanism never wired to anything*.

So the critic emits a `pattern:<slug>` per finding, from a controlled but extensible list.

**The trap, and it bit us this week:** [DRE-2527](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2527/one-work-in-progress-cap-not-four-values-across-fifteen-sites) was mis-scoped because an inventory **counted occurrences of an identifier and called it a concept**. A taxonomy applied loosely makes this metric exactly as wrong. Two findings share a pattern when the same change would prevent both — **not** when they share words. Sampling by hand to check the classification is part of the work, not optional.

### 3. Promotion — recurrence forces a remedy

* **2nd occurrence:** the ledger flags it; a candidate remedy is named.
* **3rd:** a card is filed automatically, and it must propose a **test or gate**. A rule is accepted only with a written reason why it cannot be either.
* **Nothing is promoted on a hunch.** The ledger is the evidence.

### 4. The KPIs the CEO asked for

**Primary — repeat-finding rate.** Of findings this month, the share whose pattern has been seen before. **This is the number that must fall.**

**Secondary — shift-left rate.** Findings caught by **CI** rather than by the critic. As lessons become tests, the critic should stop seeing them at all. *This is the KPI that proves the codification is real* — a rule that changed nobody's behaviour moves neither number.

**Tertiary — time-to-codify.** Days between the Nth occurrence and the test/gate landing.

**Also worth watching — recurrence after remedy.** A lesson codified as a *rule* that recurs anyway is direct evidence that the rule was the wrong instrument, and the strongest available argument for a test.

### GOODHART GUARD, and it is not optional

**We do NOT want fewer findings. We want fewer REPEATS.**

Total findings rising is fine, and often good — it means the critic is looking harder or we are shipping more. If anyone starts reading "critic findings" as a defect count to minimise, the pressure lands on the critic to find less, and we will have broken the one gate that demonstrably works. Every dashboard rendering of this must show **repeat rate**, never a raw finding count, and say why in the panel copy.

## What already exists to build on

* Every verdict is a structured qa-bot comment with a cause tag, a reviewed SHA and a content hash.
* Fix attempts are numbered and their outcomes recorded on the PR.
* Run cost and turn counts are in the logs (`num_turns`, `total_cost_usd`).
* `bureau-pipeline/standards/` is the delivery channel that already works — proven this week, when the fix agent cited `console-honesty.md` chapter and verse.

## The delivery gap to close alongside it

Standards reach **CI build agents** by injection and the `dreadnought-standards` plugin. They did **not** reach the interactive session that wrote the defect this card was born from. Same org, same knowledge, one reader short.

Whatever this builds must reach **every** surface that writes code, or we will keep proving the lesson on whichever agent did not get the memo.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Every critic finding lands in the ledger with a pattern slug, automatically
- [ ] The repeat-finding rate is computed and visible, with a stated baseline and date
- [ ] A pattern reaching its threshold files a card demanding a test or gate — a rule only with a written reason
- [ ] At least one lesson from this week is codified as a **gate** end-to-end and proven to fail CI on a reintroduction
- [ ] The dashboard shows repeat rate, never raw finding count, and says why
- [ ] A hand-sampled check confirms the pattern classification is measuring concepts, not matching words

## Why Wave 3, moved from Wave 5 on 2026-08-19

**Originally filed under Wave 5** on the reasoning that *"Layer 3 owns the gates and the critic."* Moved at the operator's direction after a day that produced three instances of one pattern.

**The Wave 5 dependency was weaker than the card claimed.** The ledger *consumes* critic output that already exists in its final form — every verdict is a structured comment with a cause tag, a reviewed SHA and a content hash; fix attempts are numbered; `num_turns` and `total_cost_usd` are in the logs. **Recording and counting needs nothing Wave 5 will build.** Only the last mile (a new `pattern:` emission from the critic) touches Wave 5's territory, and that can follow.

**Wave 3 owns *fix the record*, and a ledger of what each lesson BECAME is the record.** The ~57 stale ADRs are the same failure at rest: knowledge written once, never checked, silently wrong. This is the live version.

### The argument that actually moved it

Waiting until Wave 5 means **every rule written between now and then decays unmeasured, and Wave 5 inherits the pile.** That is structurally *"we'll fix the record last"* — the sequencing this programme already rejected when it moved the incident corpus earlier (*"Wave 2–3, not a byproduct"*).

**2026-08-19 alone produced three occurrences of one pattern** — a fact duplicated across files, fixed in one place, and asserted complete:

| Fact | Copies | Fixed |
| -- | -- | -- |
| a `#164` PR citation | 3 | 2 |
| the Actions budget runway | 2 | 1 |
| a "stack retired" note | 2 | 1 |

Under this card's own promotion rule, **the third would have auto-filed a card demanding a gate.** Instead it exists in a commit message and one person's recollection — which is precisely what the card argues is not memory.

**Deferring the mechanism that measures decay is itself the decay.**

cards.title: Alert delivery that leaves the console — push and email, wired in production
cards.description:
Phase 2 of [DRE-2531](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2531>), carrying the acceptance that phase 1 does not deliver.

**Filed because of a review finding on PR #2064, and the finding was right.** That PR ships the blocking dialog under [DRE-2531](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2531/the-console-can-raise-an-alarm-but-has-no-way-to-reach-the-ceo-both)'s own branch name, so merging it would have closed [DRE-2531](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2531/the-console-can-raise-an-alarm-but-has-no-way-to-reach-the-ceo-both) with its entire acceptance checklist untouched — `linear-sync` closes on the branch, and it does not read PR bodies that say "phase 1 of N".

That is **the same failure as** [DRE-2527](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2527/one-work-in-progress-cap-not-four-values-across-fifteen-sites) **earlier the same night**, where a card closed on merge with half its work outstanding. The rule was written down at the time — *split the card before pushing, not after; whatever ships is what the card will say* — and then not followed. Writing a rule down does not enforce it; that is Wave 4's job (finding 12, *one branch closes exactly one card*), and until it exists this is the manual discipline that substitutes for it.

## The problem, unchanged since [DRE-2531](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2531/the-console-can-raise-an-alarm-but-has-no-way-to-reach-the-ceo-both) was filed

`delivery.deliver()` fans a CRITICAL out to push and email. The logic is correct and covered by tests against **injected transports**. In production **no** `ALERT_*` **variable is set anywhere** — not in `infra/lib/backend-stack.ts`, which configures 25+ others, and nowhere else in the repo.

So `default_email_sender` logs *"alert email skipped — ALERT_SMTP_HOST not set"* and returns; `default_push_sender` logs *"alert push skipped"* and returns. **Both fail silently, at info level.** Every CRITICAL this console has ever raised has been panel-only.

The blocking dialog (phase 1) covers the case where the CEO is *looking at the console*. This covers the case where he is not — which, at 2am, is the case that matters.

## The working path already exists in this codebase

Member invites reach real inboxes today through **AWS SES** (`invite_email.SesInviteEmailSender`, gated on `INVITE_EMAIL_FROM`, which **is** set in production).

Alerts use a **different transport — raw SMTP** — that was never wired. This is not "we need email delivery." It is **two email implementations, one proven in production and one that has never executed**, and the alerts got the second.

## Scope

1. **Red first** — a test proving that with no `ALERT_*` configuration a CRITICAL raise reaches no transport and still reports success. That is today's behaviour and it should be a failing test.
2. Point alert email at the **SES sender that already works**. Delete the SMTP implementation or make it an explicit fallback; do not leave two.
3. **A missing transport must not be a silent info log.** A console that cannot deliver is itself an operator-visible condition — an alarm that cannot ring is the failure class this programme exists to remove.
4. **Decide whether budget-class WARN may leave the console.** Today `deliver()` returns early for anything below CRITICAL. An 80% warning that only lands on a screen nobody is looking at repeats the failure it was built to prevent. Either make WARN deliverable for budget kinds, or state plainly that WARN is console-only and CRITICAL is the one that reaches out.
5. Choose a channel that **actually cuts through**. Email is saturated — GitHub's own budget warning reached the CEO five days early and was missed in an inbox this pipeline had flooded.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A real CRITICAL raised in production reaches the CEO out-of-band, demonstrated once, with the receipt
- [ ] A misconfigured or missing transport is loudly visible, never an info log
- [ ] Exactly one email implementation remains
- [ ] The delivery path is exercised against something other than an injected fake

**That last one is the whole point.** Passing tests against a fake transport is exactly what this code has always had, and it is why nothing has ever been sent.

cards.title: An agent that runs out of turns should save its work and say how far it got
cards.description:
**Operator, 2026-08-19:** *"It would be great if we could use a mechanism to see how much work they had left as it got closer to that number of turns. If they have a ton of work to do and they're not even close, we should kill them earlier. If they're one or two turns away, we should not use the hard number."*

Exactly right, and it is a better idea than a bigger ceiling. [DRE-2533](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2533>) raised the fix agent 60 → 150, which makes the failure rarer; it does nothing about the fact that **when it does happen, everything is lost.**

## The operator sharpened this again, and it is a ~10x change in value

> *"We should be checking in every so often, right? Even if we've done work, we should never leave that work undone or lose that work."*

Correct, and it makes the original framing of this card too narrow. Checkpointing **only when approaching the ceiling** protects against one death out of several. Checkpointing **continuously** protects against all of them.

From the diagnosis's own census of agent deaths — **149 PRs**:

| Cause | PRs | Saved by a ceiling-only checkpoint? |
| -- | -- | -- |
| rate-limit | **86** | no |
| quota exhausted | 26 | no |
| model unavailable | 23 | no |
| **max-turns** | **14** | yes |

**A checkpoint that fires only at the turn ceiling addresses 14 of 149 deaths — under 10%.** The dominant killer is a rate-limit death, which arrives without warning at an arbitrary point and takes everything with it. An agent cannot see that coming, so there is no "approaching the limit" moment to hook.

**Periodic checkpointing is indifferent to the cause of death.** That is the whole argument: it does not need to predict the failure, and it therefore covers the 135 deaths no ceiling logic can.

### The rule

**Commit whenever the tree is in a state you would be willing to hand over.** Not every N turns — a clock is arbitrary — but at every point where the work so far stands on its own: a test written and failing for the right reason, a fix made and its suite green, a file understood and a note recorded. That is also the honest definition of a checkpoint: *if I vanished right now, is what I leave behind useful to whoever comes next?*

### The hazard to design around — a checkpoint must not re-trigger the gates

Preserving work means PUSHING it: an unpushed commit dies with the runner, so committing locally solves nothing. But every push to a PR branch re-triggers the critic and CI. Twenty checkpoints in a run would mean twenty reviews, which is a far more expensive failure than the one being fixed.

The clean answer is to push checkpoints to a ref no workflow watches — `refs/wip/<branch>` — so the work is durable on the remote while the gates stay quiet. A resuming run reads that ref and continues; the branch itself only moves when the agent has something it is prepared to have reviewed. Pushing checkpoints straight to the PR branch would trade a lost-work problem for a review-storm problem, and must not be the implementation.

## What is and is not possible

**Not possible: extending the budget mid-run.** `--max-turns` is a hard ceiling inside `claude-code-action`. Nothing outside the process can grant more turns to a run already in flight, so "if they are one or two turns away, let them finish" cannot be implemented as written. Worth saying plainly rather than designing around a capability we do not have.

**Possible, and it gets the same outcome by a different route: make the loss recoverable.** The reason "one or two turns away" hurts is that hitting the wall discards everything. If the agent commits what it has and records what remains, then being cut short costs the remainder rather than the whole run — and the next dispatch resumes instead of restarting from turn one against the same wall.

That converts the hard ceiling from a cliff into a checkpoint, which is what the request is really asking for.

**Possible: killing early on no progress.** Half-exists already — [DRE-2024](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2024/reconcile-re-dispatches-a-doomed-agent-fix-every-sweep-for-a-needs) halts after two runs that ended with the no-progress marker on the same head sha. What is missing is the *within-run* version: an agent 60% through its budget having edited nothing is not going to finish, and should stop rather than spend the rest.

## The mechanism

The agent already reads a prompt and writes files. Both halves can be done there, with no change to the action:

1. **A progress checkpoint.** Instruct the agent that on approaching its budget it must (a) commit whatever compiles and passes, even if partial, and (b) write `/tmp/fix-progress.md` naming what is done, what remains, and what it would do next.
2. **The Report step reads it.** A partial commit plus a stated remainder becomes a PR comment and the input to the next attempt — so the loop resumes with context rather than rediscovering it.
3. **The halt decides on evidence, not just repetition.** [DRE-2024](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2024/reconcile-re-dispatches-a-doomed-agent-fix-every-sweep-for-a-needs) currently counts identical no-progress runs. With a stated remainder it can distinguish *"90% done, one test failing"* — worth another attempt — from *"has not understood the diff"* — stop and escalate. That is the operator's "kill them earlier" with something real to judge on.
4. **Then the ceiling matters much less**, and 150 could reasonably come back down. A budget only has to cover *a useful increment* once increments accumulate.

## Why this is worth more than the number

A `--max-turns` death commits nothing today. PR #2063 burned twelve minutes and $10.67 across two runs and left no trace of what either learned — the second attempt began exactly where the first did, and hit the wall at the same place. **The waste is not the ceiling, it is the amnesia.**

## Scope

1. **Red first** — a test proving that a run stopped at its ceiling leaves a commit and a stated remainder, rather than nothing.
2. Prompt instruction: checkpoint and record before the budget is gone.
3. Report step: surface the remainder on the PR and feed it to the next attempt.
4. Teach [DRE-2024](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2024/reconcile-re-dispatches-a-doomed-agent-fix-every-sweep-for-a-needs)'s halt to read the remainder, so *nearly done* and *hopelessly stuck* stop being the same signal.
5. Re-evaluate the ceiling once increments accumulate — 150 may then be more than needed.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A fix run stopped at its ceiling leaves a commit and a written remainder
- [ ] The next attempt starts from that commit, provably — not from the original head
- [ ] A run making no progress can be stopped before its budget is spent
- [ ] [DRE-2024](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2024/reconcile-re-dispatches-a-doomed-agent-fix-every-sweep-for-a-needs)'s halt still fires for a genuinely non-converging loop
- [ ] Demonstrated on a real PR, not only in the workflow file

## The resuming agent MUST be free to throw the checkpoint away

**Operator:** *"The repair agent, the next one that picks it up, will notice what it's done and will either say it's shit or it's good, right?"*

It will **see** the work — it is on the branch. It will **not judge** it unless we say so, and that distinction decides whether this feature helps or hurts.

Today's fix prompt says: read the verdict, read the failing CI, fix. Nothing tells an agent that some of the code in front of it is a **predecessor's unfinished attempt** rather than the deliberate state of the branch. Absent that, the natural reading of existing code is that someone meant it — so a resuming agent would build *on top of* a half-finished idea instead of assessing it.

**That is how checkpointing turns from preserving progress into compounding error.** Attempt 2 inherits attempt 1's wrong turn, attempt 3 inherits both, and each one looks more deliberate than the last.

So the resume contract needs three things, and they are as load-bearing as the checkpoint itself:

1. **Say it is a checkpoint.** The resuming agent must be told explicitly that the work is unfinished, whose it was, and that it is a proposal rather than a decision.
2. **Judge it before extending it.** First action on resume is to assess: is this heading the right way? The stated remainder (`what I did / what remains / what I would do next`) is what makes that judgement cheap — without it the agent must reverse-engineer intent from a diff, which costs the very turns the checkpoint saved.
3. **Discarding is a legitimate outcome, and must be said out loud.** *"I read the previous attempt, it was going the wrong way, I reverted it and started again"* has to be an approved answer. If the prompt implies the checkpoint must be preserved, we have built a ratchet that only accumulates.

**A checkpoint is a handover note, not an inheritance.** The value is that the next agent starts informed — including informed enough to reject it.

## TESTING BAR — this card does not ship on unit tests

**Operator, 2026-08-19:** *"This is a very sensitive and delicate area. Do we really want to test the heck out of this and do scenario and adversarial tests against this?"* Yes. Recorded as a condition of the card, not a preference.

**Why this one is different from everything else shipped this week.** Every other change was either incapable of breaking anything (a turn ceiling can only let an agent run longer) or provable at rest (a constant, a selector, a persisted token). This one changes **what agents DO**: what they commit, where they push, and how the next agent treats what it finds. That behaviour exists only in a live run. A green unit suite here proves the helper functions work, not that the mechanism is safe.

And it changes the posture of every write: today an agent's commit is a **deliberate** act at the end of reasoning. A checkpoint is an **automatic** commit of whatever the working tree happens to hold. Those are not the same risk.

### Scenario tests — the whole path, not the pieces

1. Agent works, dies at the ceiling → the checkpoint exists on the wip ref AND the remainder is written.
2. The next run resumes from the checkpoint, finishes the job, and pushes to the PR branch — with the PR's history still readable.
3. A run that dies to a **rate-limit** (86 of 149 deaths — the real case) checkpoints identically. If it only works for max-turns we built the 10% version.
4. A run that finishes normally produces **no** wip ref and no behaviour change at all — the common path must be untouched.

### Adversarial tests — what breaks it

1. **The ratchet.** Seed a checkpoint that went the WRONG way. The next agent must be able to reject and revert it, and must say so. If it silently builds on top, the feature makes the pipeline worse and must not ship.
2. **The review storm.** N checkpoints must trigger **zero** extra critic/CI runs. Assert the trigger count, not the intent.
3. **A checkpoint must never be mergeable.** Green CI plus a stale APPROVE against a checkpoint must not merge. `merge-gate` anchors a verdict to the reviewed SHA and treats a stale one as no verdict — prove that still holds with checkpoints in play, rather than assuming it.
4. **Secrets.** A checkpoint commits *whatever is in the tree*, including a scratch file an agent wrote mid-debug. A token-shaped string must never reach a ref. `claude_reconnect`'s `_SECRET_SHAPED` scrubbing is the existing precedent. **This is the highest-severity failure on the list** — everything else costs money or time.
5. **Half-applied work.** A checkpoint that does not build must not be committed, or must be unmissably marked as broken.
6. **Concurrency.** `agent-fix` runs with `cancel-in-progress: false`, so two runs can be live on one PR. Two checkpoints racing the same wip ref must not clobber or interleave into nonsense.
7. **Diverged base.** A human pushes to the PR branch while a wip ref exists from an older base. Resuming onto a moved base must fail safe, not silently re-apply stale work.
8. **Ref hygiene.** Wip refs must be cleaned up on merge/close, or the repo accumulates them forever.
9. **Death mid-checkpoint.** Killed while committing or pushing — the ref must be either the old state or the new one, never half.

### And it must be rehearsed before the fleet sees it

Unit and scenario coverage is necessary and not sufficient: the failure modes above are behavioural and cross-run. This needs a live rehearsal in `bureau-harness` — the sandbox that exists for exactly this and is currently switched off with its own fix unproven. So this card is **gated on Wave 1**: the release channel (so a bad engine change is one command to revert) and a working sandbox (so it is rehearsed before eight repos run it).

Shipping this to `@main` without both would be the largest single risk taken in this programme so far, and would contradict the rule the programme was written to enforce: *nothing reaches the fleet that the sandbox has not rehearsed.*

## Risk to respect

A partial commit must never leave the branch worse than it found it — half-applied edits that fail CI are harder to reason about than no edits. The checkpoint should commit only what passes, and say so; "committed nothing, here is why" is a legitimate and useful outcome.

And the same risk in the other direction: a checkpoint that LOOKS finished is worse than one that announces itself as partial. Whatever marks it — the ref it lives on, the commit subject, the progress note — must be unmissable to the next reader, human or agent.

cards.title: [WAVE 7] Layer 5 — Console refresh, over signals now known to be honest
cards.description:
**Wave 7 of 8.** A visual refresh, as scoped by the CEO — **designed during waves 2–5, built here.** Design work may run ahead; nothing else may.

Gated on Layer 0 truth holding in production, not on the intervening waves: a beautiful console over untrustworthy state is worse than a plain one.

> **Amended 2026-08-30.** Three of this epic's five scope bullets described a world that no longer exists, so they are corrected here rather than left to send the next reader after finished work. Every figure below was **measured on **`main` **on 2026-08-30**, not carried across.
>
> * The 24 catalogued gaps are BUILT. `console/design/DESIGN-IMPACT-2026-06-13.md` is a June snapshot. Its gaps were carded the same day as thirteen area cards under [DRE-1441](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-1441/epic-console-design-clean-up-fidelity-divergences-design-vs-as-built), and **all thirteen are Done**. Spot-checked in the tree: the top-bar title is `text-xl` (was `text-sm`), the bare `24m` shipped and cites [DRE-1460](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-1460/console-design-card-flyout-shared-header-phase-gauge-inline-drop-age) in its own comment, the redundant `FLEET` eyebrow is gone, and the sidebar renders a real `ProjectDot` rather than a generic star. The catalogue is history, not a work list.
> * `ui/workbench` **has landed.** The bullet called it "the estate's worst long-lived-branch violation" at 22 commits and +21,463 lines. It is now **0 commits ahead of **`origin/main` — [DRE-2521](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2521/land-the-atomic-component-library-from-uiworkbench), [DRE-2522](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2522/land-the-design-coverage-audits-and-token-vocabularies) and [DRE-2523](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2523/land-the-clickable-console-prototype-from-uiworkbench) landed it. Nothing to split.
> * **The read layer moved out of this epic.** The honesty work these screens depend on is [DRE-2822](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2822/epic-the-system-can-be-read-what-is-happening-who-acts-next-and-what), condensed into **Phase 6**, with the two deferred mode-3 surfaces ([DRE-2852](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2852/moving-work-looks-like-it-is-moving-a-pulse-earned-from-a-timestamp), [DRE-2853](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2853/receipts-ride-the-push-channel-the-console-learns-in-seconds-not-on)) in Phase 7. This epic no longer owns it.

## Scope — what is actually left

> **Amended 2026-09-03.** The **home page** is not in this epic. It was designed with the CEO over two sessions ([DRE-3010](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-3010>), [DRE-3049](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-3049>)) and is built by [DRE-3060](<https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-3060>) — a sibling epic, not a child, because a home-page rebuild and this epic's cleanup share no files. This epic keeps the token work, the signed-out screens, the component-vocabulary duplication and the dead `/portfolio/*` routes.

* **Apply the design system consistently.** Still a strength: 121 tokens, mirrored and test-guarded. Measured 2026-08-30: **139 raw colour literals across 16 non-test files** — and **six of those files are the signed-out screens**, which is the concentration, not a spread.
* **Fix the signed-out screens** — the one surface still off the token system. `pages/auth/` carries 32 hex literals across `SignIn`, `SignUp`, `CheckEmail`, `ForgotPassword`, `ResetPassword` and `OAuthRow`. This is the single largest remaining fidelity gap and it is the first screen anyone sees.
* **Resolve the duplication:** two component vocabularies — `components/atoms/` (60 files) and `components/ui/` (13) — plus a hand-written mobile component tree that has drifted from its desktop twin.
* **Four unreachable **`/portfolio/*` **routes.** Confirmed unreachable 2026-08-30: they mount `NodeView` under `EngineLayout`, but the live drill-down is `/engine` (`ENGINE_BASE`), and **no **`to=` **or **`href=` **anywhere in the app points at **`/portfolio`. Dead routes, still built and shipped.

## Quiet level

0. 

## Exit test

Every number on the dashboard traces to a source Layer 0 proved honest. The screens match their designs.

## Demo — a week, not a session

You use the console for a week of real work. Then, on demand, **any number traced to its source**. **Fails if** there is a number you do not believe, or a screen you avoid because the old one was easier.

cards.title: [WAVE 6] Layer 4 — Refactor where the evidence says, behind the corpus
cards.description:
**Wave 6 of 8.** Only possible because the incident corpus exists — you cannot safely refactor a state machine you cannot regression-test.

**This wave is a decision, not a given.** Refactor-or-keep-patching is decided per module, on numbers.

## Scope

* Correlate fix-churn × complexity × incident density per module, then decide: refactor with a named boundary, or keep patching **with a stated reason**
* Candidates: `console/backend/schema.py` (8,798 lines, 478 classes, 268 functions, **26 fix commits**), `store.py` (3,424 / 18), `sources.py` (1,846 / 18)
* **The Claude-account concept** — one idea across three stores with **68 fix commits**, the worst cluster in the codebase
* The open question: whether the state machine stays as **5,596 lines of workflow YAML** (`qa-review.yml` alone is 1,264) or moves into tested code the workflows merely call
* **Extend the pattern already invented** — one source, generated mirrors between markers, a `--check` in CI — to the two thirds of configuration still governed by comments that merely *assert* agreement. Three such comments are false today.
* Drive unguarded duplicates to zero

## Quiet level

0 — the console deploys independently of the pipeline.

## Exit test

The corpus passes **identically** before and after. Every candidate has a written decision. The highest-churn file is no longer the file every change must touch.

## Demo

The corpus run before and after, results diffed side by side. **Fails if any fixture had to be edited to pass** — if a fixture changed, behaviour changed, and this was not a refactor.

cards.title: [WAVE 5] Layer 3 — Gates and the critic: every verdict gets an owner
cards.description:
**Wave 5 of 8.** Recovers pure wasted spend, and closes the last of the 20 unwatched stall modes.

## Scope

* **The pull-request-keyed clock** — designed 2026-08-13 in `adr-gate-repair-and-stall-detection.md`, named as the load-bearing fix, still marked Proposed with nothing built. Every backstop today keys on a card in one of four lanes; the pull request that holds the code is watched only by report-only alerts.
* A change request gets an owner **on every branch**, or the branch is refused up front
* **Retries must vary something.** The medic re-runs the same run id with an identical payload, commit, model and secrets — confirmed three times over seven weeks. One instance burned $4.05 for no verdict; another $20.48 across 151 turns for no pull request.
* Make `cancelled`, `timed_out` and `skipped` visible to the medic. They are structurally invisible today — and they are exactly what every job timeout and every `cancel-in-progress` produces.
* One diagnosis card per root cause. One card has absorbed 14 diagnoses across five unrelated causes; nine such cards are live at a median age of 500 hours.
* **Batching becomes a property of the machine**: review on ready-for-review, not on every push. One observed PR drew six reviews across five pushes, one cancelled mid-flight — tokens spent, no verdict, head left mute.
* Retire the 5 of 16 watchdog signatures that have never fired once — dead detection reads as coverage
* **Decide with evidence whether the judge should be as strong as the builder.** Builders run Opus 5; critic, verifier and medic run Sonnet 5. Since no human reads the diff, a defect the critic misses looks identical to a clean approval. Measurable: count approvals that later needed a repair. *(Quota isolation is already shipped — the critic mints from a separate bucket since the June incident.)*

## Quiet level

1, with a brief 2 for the medic change.

## Exit test

Each of the 20 unwatched stall modes has a watcher, or a written and accepted reason for not having one. A retry that cannot vary its inputs is not attempted.

## Demo

I open a PR with a real defect on a **badly named branch** — it is still gated and still gets an owner. I make a run time out and the medic sees it, which today is impossible. A retry with identical inputs is **refused rather than attempted**. **Fails if** any of the 20 modes can still go dark.

cards.title: [WAVE 4] Layer 2 — The state machine (87% of the cost)
cards.description:
**Wave 4 of 8. The biggest wave by cards recovered, and the only one needing a maintenance window.**

## Scope

* **Backlog gets a watcher.** 116 of 138 live cards sit in a lane nothing looks at; ~104 stalled cards were never dispatched at all.
* **The card contract enforced at the door** — auto-repair where labels can be inferred, refuse where they cannot. Unlabelled cards complete 49% of the time against 76–92%. A refusal is immediate and self-explaining, which is strictly better than today's park-in-an-unwatched-lane.
* **Intake moves off the CEO's desk.** He describes intent; cards are written for him, dedupe-checked, correctly labelled. He confirms one line about intent, never structure.
* **Close the escalation loop.** Today `agent-task.yml` says "answer here and the agent picks up your guidance" — but the prompt interpolates only title and description, comments are never fetched, and the console's retry writes no guidance at all. He answers, the agent re-reads an identical card, and asks again.
* **Delete** `Plan Review` in ONE coordinated change: the sweep's `PARKED_STATE`, the pipeline tests naming it, and the console page. It has never held a card in 1,750. Backlog-plus-held becomes the one honest queue. *Do not simply delete the lane in Linear.*
* One owner each for `Todo` (7+ writers today), `In QA` (3), and epic close (two independent implementations with different definitions of "finished")
* Hand-work becomes reconcilable rather than a permanent stall; operator cards route to the operator, not to an engineer agent

## Quiet level

**2 — one drain window, after 21:00 PT.** Lane ownership cannot change safely while cards move through it. Median cycle 27 min, p90 3.2h, so four hours clears ~90%. Only safe because Layer 0 can now prove when in-flight is empty.

## Exit test

No card can enter a lane with no owner responsible for getting it out.

## Demo — tier 3, the hardest bar

**You describe one real piece of work in your own words and walk away.** It completes. Then one that *should* stop and ask — you answer once and it finishes **without asking again**. Then you try to file something unlabelled and watch it refused at the door with a reason. **Fails if** you are asked the same question twice, or you touch anything on the "not your job" list to get it finished.

cards.description:
**Wave 2 of 8.** Nothing else in this programme can be trusted until this lands.

## Scope

* The sweep's status reflects **fleet health**, not sweep completion (it reported success ~40 times across a 14-hour jam)
* A run's conclusion may not contradict a check it published — the discrepancy that hid the jam behind a green signal
* **The 13 silent gate exits leave durable evidence, including "declined, and why."** Prerequisite for the one-screen view: you cannot display a reason the gate never recorded.
* Every stall names **one** cause. A watchdog that does not know says so rather than guessing — it guessed wrong on all five portico cards, and the run it claimed had not started opened a PR 40 minutes later.
* Close the Done-without-a-merge-receipt hole, **with the operator-card carve-out** (an operator card legitimately has no merge; without the exemption this becomes a false-alarm generator)
* **The stage-transition record** — one durable row per transition. This single build yields three things: the one-screen card view, the four walk-away metrics, and the incident-corpus fixture format.
* **Start the incident corpus.** 16 fixtures are writable from the diagnosis today. Moved earlier than originally planned because Layer 4 cannot proceed without it.

## Quiet level

1 — frozen channel.

## Execution

Best sub-agent fan-out in the programme: the 16 corpus fixtures are independent, one per incident, each with its own failing test. The gate-evidence and honest-status work stays by hand — subtle, and everything rests on it.

## Corpus rules

Every fixture demonstrated **red first**, asserting *desired* not observed behaviour. A test currently pins the banned model in place; do not industrialise that mistake 16 times. Fixtures assert **behaviour, not implementation**, or the corpus blocks the refactor it exists to enable.

## Exit test

Replay the jam: within one sweep interval, exactly one surface names the five cards, the PR, and the real reason — with no human reading a log.

## Demo

**You pick any card**, past or present, and explain its entire life in one minute on one screen. **Fails if** you need to open GitHub or read a log, or if any field reads "unknown" where a decision was actually made.

cards.title: Flip the portal CSP from Report-Only to enforcing — author the policy, hand the operator the command
cards.description:
The last unfinished phase of OPERATOR MILESTONE 4 ([DRE-2233](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2233/operator-milestone-4-content-pipeline-live-legacy-stubs-csp-enforcing)), scoped to one PR and brought onto the current release path. Everything else in that milestone is verified done: the content pipeline is live, and the per-project access cutover is complete — no `grant#root#g:<project>` bridge grant remains in any of the seven projects across both accounts (measured 2026-08-17).

Measured live 2026-08-17: `share.gridcorr.com` and `share.everybite.com` return `content-security-policy-report-only` and no enforcing header.

## What ships in this PR

Author the enforcing counterpart to the existing Report-Only setup. **No AWS call is made by this card** — agents author `infra/cdn/` scripts and never run them.

* A new policy document beside `infra/cdn/csp-policy.json`, carrying the identical directive string, as the **enforcing** header.
* `infra/cdn/11-csp-enforce-policy.sh`, modelled directly on `10-csp-report-only-policy.sh` — same `--profile` contract, same converge-don't-duplicate behaviour, same operator-only header comment.
* A rollback script, or a documented `--report-only` flag on the same script, that puts a distribution back. Rollback must be one command and must be written down before the forward step, per the house rule.
* Tests in `infra/test/cdn_scripts.test.ts` alongside the existing coverage.

**Use the real enforcing mechanism, deliberately chosen and written down.** `10-csp-report-only-policy.sh`'s header explains that the Report-Only header is a CUSTOM header specifically because `SecurityHeadersConfig.ContentSecurityPolicy` is the enforcing field. State in the script which of the two this uses and why, so the next reader does not have to rediscover the distinction.

## Release path — this is why it never moved

The CSP is not shipped by `cdk deploy` and not by the SPA publish. It is an account-level CloudFront `ResponseHeadersPolicy` applied by a shell script and attached by `30-content-behavior.sh`. It is a **third release path**, which is exactly why everything else advanced and this did not. The PR must hand the operator the literal commands, per account and per distribution, in order — and say plainly that merging this changes nothing until they are run.

## The blast radius

The policy string was authored at P1-D2 and has not changed; the SPA is 100+ commits newer. A wrong enforcing CSP takes the portal shell dark for every reader in that account, and [DRE-2233](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2233/operator-milestone-4-content-pipeline-live-legacy-stubs-csp-enforcing)'s own warning is that a CSP which breaks live documents gets switched off in a hurry — leaving the platform with no CSP at all, worse than the starting position. That is why the evidence card comes first.

**Scope is the portal shell.** The sandboxed frame carries its own CSP from `sanitize_lib.ts` at an opaque origin. Not this card; do not touch it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An enforcing policy document exists carrying a directive string **byte-identical** to `infra/cdn/csp-policy.json`'s, with a test asserting the two cannot drift
- [ ] `infra/cdn/11-csp-enforce-policy.sh` follows `10-csp-report-only-policy.sh`'s shape: `--profile` argument, converges rather than duplicating, and an OPERATOR-ONLY header stating agents never run it
- [ ] Rollback to Report-Only is one documented command, present in the same PR as the forward step
- [ ] The script states which CloudFront field carries the enforcing header and why, rather than leaving the custom-vs-`SecurityHeadersConfig` choice implicit
- [ ] `infra/test/cdn_scripts.test.ts` covers the new script; `npm test` and `npm run typecheck` clean
- [ ] The PR body carries the exact operator commands per account and per distribution, in order, and states that merging changes nothing live until they run
- [ ] `docs/runbooks/cdn.md` "The CSP soak" is updated to describe the flip and its rollback
- [ ] No AWS CLI write is performed by this card

cards.title: The share panel tells the truth about documents Portico cannot gate
cards.description:
> **Branch:** `agent/DRE-2498-<slug>`**.** Not `ui/*`, not `feat/*`, and **not the** `sid/dre-2498-…` **name Linear suggests** — `linear-sync.yml` reads the card id out of the merged branch, so any other prefix means this card does not close itself. `hand-built` decides who writes the code, not where it lands. One card, one branch, one PR. **This epic has already lost one card to that mistake** — [DRE-2495](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2495/the-external-document-screen-open-in-a-new-tab-and-say-who-controls) merged as `ui/forms-spec` and had to be closed by hand.

> **AMENDED 2026-08-22 — scope widened, because there are now three answers, not two.** The share panel has to tell the truth about **every** item kind, and the truth differs:
>
> * a **Google Doc** — *Google decides who can open this. Portico cannot.*
> * a **form** ([DRE-2628](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2628/epic-forms-a-form-is-its-own-object-in-portico)) — *the people granted on this folder can open it*, which is Portico's own gate and fully enforced
> * everything Portico hosts — as today
>
> A single sentence covering all three will be wrong for two of them. Fork the copy by kind.
>
> Now `hand-built` — built locally and looked at before committing.

**Blocked by:** [DRE-2494](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2494/add-a-document-by-link-without-fetching-it-the-row-the-route-and-a)

The disclosure half of the epic's accepted risk, at the place where a moderator forms a belief about who can read what.

## The specific false belief to prevent

A moderator opens the share panel, sees the grant list, and reasonably concludes *these are the people who can read these documents.* For a link-out document that is **not true** — Google's sharing decides, and Portico cannot see it.

The sharper case is revocation. Remove a partner and the panel shows them gone. Their Portico documents really are gone. **The Google link in their history still works, and nothing on this screen says so.**

The epic accepts two access systems on the explicit condition that this is disclosed rather than hidden. [DRE-2495](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2495/the-external-document-screen-open-in-a-new-tab-and-say-who-controls) covers the document; this covers the moderator's mental model, which is where the damage actually starts.

## Behaviour

* Where a folder or root contains link-out documents, the share panel says that some documents in it open outside Portico and are not governed by these grants.
* On removing someone's access, if any link-out document is in scope, say plainly that access to externally-hosted files must be revoked where those files live. Once, at the moment of the action — not a standing banner people learn to skim.
* Name the count and let the moderator see which documents, so the follow-up is actionable rather than a vague worry.

## Deliberately NOT in scope

**Do not check, read, or reconcile Google's permissions.** That needs the Google credential the epic refuses. This card discloses; it does not enforce, and an "are these in sync?" indicator would be a lie without an API call.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The share panel discloses when its scope contains documents Portico does not gate, with a count
- [ ] Removing access surfaces the external-file caveat at the moment of removal, when any link-out document is in scope
- [ ] A moderator can see which documents these are
- [ ] Nothing claims or implies Portico knows the external sharing state
- [ ] A folder with no link-out documents shows no new copy at all — this must not become noise on every share
- [ ] No Google API call added

cards.title: Add-document: paste a Google link and choose to link to it, not copy it
cards.description:
> **Branch:** `agent/DRE-2497-<slug>`**.** Not `ui/*`, not `feat/*`, and **not the** `sid/dre-2497-…` **name Linear suggests** — `linear-sync.yml` reads the card id out of the merged branch, so any other prefix means this card does not close itself. `hand-built` decides who writes the code, not where it lands. One card, one branch, one PR. **This epic has already lost one card to that mistake** — [DRE-2495](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2495/the-external-document-screen-open-in-a-new-tab-and-say-who-controls) merged as `ui/forms-spec` and had to be closed by hand.

> **AMENDED 2026-08-22 — file collision, and this card is now** `hand-built`**.** [DRE-2634](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2634/a4-place-a-form-into-a-customer-folder-from-the-library) **(A4, place a form into a customer folder) edits the same two surfaces**: `LibraryScreen.tsx` and `AddDocumentModal/`, where `linkLogic.ts` and `linkTransport.ts` already sit.
>
> **Do not run the two concurrently.** Whoever starts second rebases on the first. Both are `hand-built` so they queue behind one person rather than being split across a dispatched agent and a local one — which is how two agents produce one conflict on a single surface.
>
> `hand-built` also because the add-and-place flow is a drag interaction, and drag behaviour does not survive being described in a ticket and checked by a test.

**Blocked by:** [DRE-2494](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2494/add-a-document-by-link-without-fetching-it-the-row-the-route-and-a)

The moderator-facing half: paste a URL and say which of the two things you mean.

## The distinction the UI must make honest

There are now two URL behaviours and they are easy to confuse:

* **Copy it into Portico** (exists today) — we fetch the page and serve our own snapshot. Gated, versioned, anchorable comments. Only works for ordinary HTML pages.
* **Link to it where it lives** ([DRE-2494](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2494/add-a-document-by-link-without-fetching-it-the-row-the-route-and-a)) — we store a pointer. Opens in a new tab, Google's comments, **outside Portico's gate**.

`AddDocumentModal/linkLogic.ts:176` currently states the first as an unconditional fact: *"We fetch a copy and serve it from Portico."* That sentence becomes wrong for half the flows the moment [DRE-2494](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2494/add-a-document-by-link-without-fetching-it-the-row-the-route-and-a) lands, so it has to become conditional on the choice.

## Behaviour

* Detect a Google Docs/Sheets/Slides URL and **default to link-out** — fetching one is never right; it snapshots a sign-in page. `normalizeExt` (`infra/lambda/items_lib.ts:262`) already sniffs Google Sheets URLs into `gsheet`; reuse that rather than writing a second matcher.
* For an ordinary URL, offer both, defaulting to today's copy-into-Portico behaviour so nothing existing changes under the moderator.
* State the consequence **before** the commit, which is this codebase's own standard (see `Composer.tsx`'s header): a link-out document will open outside Portico and Portico will not control who can read it.
* The moderator types the title. Portico cannot read it from Google and must not pretend to.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Pasting a Google Docs/Sheets/Slides URL defaults to link-out, with the choice visible and changeable
- [ ] Pasting an ordinary page URL still defaults to today's copy-into-Portico behaviour — existing flow unchanged, asserted by a test
- [ ] The explanatory copy is conditional on the chosen mode; no screen claims we fetch a copy when we are storing a pointer
- [ ] The access consequence is stated before the moderator commits, not after
- [ ] A created link-out document appears in the library with the right icon and opens the external pane
- [ ] Errors from the route surface to the moderator and **do not discard typed input** (see [DRE-2478](https://linear.app/dreadnoughtfoundry/issue/DRE-2478/a-failed-comment-post-tells-the-reader-it-saved-post-is-the-one-call) — same failure class, same repo, this month)
